name: Almost Black
lede: Almost Black is a crowd-sourced name for a near-black with a faint green-teal cast, a color that painters, dyers and glassmakers keep meeting at the dark end of other colors.

sections.title: A name made by a survey
sections.body:
The name Almost Black comes from the 2010 xkcd color survey, where thousands of volunteers typed their own names for screen colors [1]. It is not an old pigment or dye name, and no book in our collection treats it as one [1]. Its place in the ISCC-NBS system is the block called brownish black, about 3.8 units away on the CIEDE2000 scale [1].

The swatch sits next to [[black]] and shares its job: it is the darkest end of the page, with only a trace of hue left. That is also how books use the phrase. They reach for "almost black" when a strong color goes dark enough that its hue is hard to name [2][3].

sections.title: Colors that go almost black
sections.body:
Several books use the phrase for colors that are really something else seen in the dark. Ruby glass transmits so little light that it looks nearly black unless it is flashed onto clear glass or lightened with colorless glass [4]. A modern dioxazine violet paint is so loaded with pigment that, squeezed from the tube, the purple looks almost black [5]. Cochineal dye shifts with tin and other additives, and the darkest reds it gives are close to black [6].

In the dyer's world the same thing happens with purple. Finlay describes Pliny's purple as an almost-black that gives a glimpse of another color in the right light [7]. The lesson is that near-black is often a deep chroma in disguise, and a change in light brings the hue back [4][7].

sections.title: When paint goes dark
sections.body:
Time can also take a color to almost black. Copper-resin greens used in the late fifteenth century darkened as the resins decomposed in light, and foliage in paintings of that era is now deep brown or almost black [8]. Ball compares the effect to a Magritte-style trick of the light [8]. Pastoureau notes that in Romanesque images artists could paint the devil in any dark color; one church ceiling gives him dark blue, almost black, fur [9].

Context matters too. Next to fresh snow, even ordinary water looks almost black, though it is no darker than on a summer day [10]. The eye judges dark against its neighbors, not in isolation [10].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color near this swatch appears in 3,604 works, or 15.2 per cent, which makes it more common than 99 per cent of the named colors [11]. It peaks in the 1600s, at 17.2 per cent of the paintings from that century [11]. Several Dutch portraitists use it heavily; Nicolaes Maes has it in 15 of 21 works in the archive [12]. Within a painting it behaves as a shadow color [12].

These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so many of those near-blacks began as browns and greens [11][8]. Read them as screen colors, not pigment tests [11].

questions.q: Why does a saturated color like ruby glass or dioxazine violet sometimes look almost black?
choices: It carries so much pigment or absorbs so much light that little of its hue gets through
It is a different color when wet
